title: Case: NovaConsulting
text: NovaConsulting is a European management consultancy with around 2,000 employees, mainly operating in Paris, Berlin, and Madrid. The firm has built a strong reputation for delivering digital transformation projects, but in recent years it has struggled to attract and retain young professionals.

Despite offering competitive salaries, NovaConsulting's recruitment results have been disappointing: application numbers from top universities are falling, and rejection rates of job offers have increased. Exit interviews suggest that candidates and employees perceive the company as “traditional” and less appealing than newer competitors who emphasize flexibility, sustainability, and employee well-being.

In response, the HR department launched an employer branding campaign centered on NovaConsulting's long history, its prestigious list of clients in the financial and industrial sectors, and its reputation for rigorous professional standards. The campaign has been visible on LinkedIn, company websites, and university job fairs, where recruiters present NovaConsulting as “a place to build a solid career through excellence and discipline.”

Recruitment is mainly conducted through a narrow set of elite universities in Europe, with assessment centers focusing heavily on cognitive ability tests and individual case interviews. Candidates who fit the “classic consultant profile” – strong analytical skills, excellent academic records, and the ability to work long hours – are prioritized. While this strategy has traditionally yielded high-caliber recruits, it has also created a relatively homogeneous workforce in terms of background, mindset, and career expectations. However, this approach no longer seems to resonate with many younger professionals.

At the same time, NovaConsulting is reconsidering its performance management system. For decades, the firm relied on a classic “up-or-out” model: consultants were evaluated once a year and either promoted, retained at the same level, or asked to leave. The evaluation process is based on feedback from project managers and partners, combined with billable hours and client satisfaction scores. While this system once reinforced a strong performance-driven culture and rapid career progression, it is now generating growing dissatisfaction.

Younger employees argue that the system rewards visibility and long hours more than collaboration, innovation, or mentoring. In a hybrid work environment, some consultants who work remotely feel disadvantaged compared to those who are more present in the office, where their efforts are more visible to managers. Managers themselves report difficulties in evaluating contributions consistently, given the team-based nature of consulting projects and the reliance on subjective judgments. Several partners worry that the model fuels stress, undermines cooperation, and drives high turnover, which is costly for the firm.

Senior leadership now faces two key HR challenges: how to redesign recruitment and employer branding to attract diverse and motivated candidates, and how to adapt performance management practices to ensure fairness and motivation in a hybrid workplace.
